messages.subject: Lavaan - credible software?
messages.subject_clean: Lavaan - credible software?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have been using Lavaan for a couple of years since I found this software is incredibly useful and helpful. I would like to use it throughout my future academic life. I also have been employing it in developing several manuscripts to publish my work to highly respected journals. Recently, I've got a comment from a professor saying that

"Lavaan only approximates SEM and even the creator of the program himself admits that “the results of lavaan are very close … to those reported by their current commercial program” (Rosseel, 2012). If lavaan does give the same results, then there really is no concern, the problem is, you never know when it may or may not."

I was not able to make an argument to the comment. I would like to ask your advice for the matters of how much this software is reliable compared to commercial softwares.

Thank you very much for your advice!

Best regards,
Yonghwan Chang

messages.body_plain:
Hi

The same question was asked on this list a couple of months ago.

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/Yfewh9tnH04

If you must have results that are results that are always identical to software X, then you must use software X. Because the estimation algorithms can be implemented in different ways, it is unlikely that software Y will always produce exactly same results as software X. This applies to Lavaan and all commercial software. For example, you cannot expect e.g. Mplus and AMOS to always give exactly the same result.

Mikko

messages.body_plain:
On 04/01/2015 06:15 AM, Experimental study with SEM wrote:
> Recently, I've got a comment from a professor saying that
>
> "Lavaan only approximates SEM

I wonder what this means "approximating SEM".

> and even the creator of the program
> himself admits that “the results of lavaan are very close … to those
> reported by their current commercial program” (Rosseel, 2012).

Your professor clearly failed to see/understand the subtle message in
this sentence: there are indeed some (minor and major) discrepancies
between lavaan and some commercial packages. I spent a lot of effort in
trying to pinpoint the cause of these discrepancies (hint: the mimic=
option). Apart from some trivial numerical issues (like the stopping
criteria used by optimizers), it turns out there are a few mistakes (or
at least non-standard implementations) in several commercial packages.

> If lavaan
> does give the same results, then there really is no concern, the problem
> is, you never know when it may or may not."

Well, this is the thing: with lavaan (or any other open-source software
for that matter), you *can* know when there is reason for concern: you
can check the source code. Many people (including SEM experts) do.

> I was not able to make an argument to the comment. I would like to ask
> your advice for the matters of how much this software is reliable
> compared to commercial softwares.

Everywhere around the world, you will find people that simply can not
believe that an open-source software package can be reliable... It is a
free world. If they prefer to buy commercial, that is fine by me.

(PS: For what it is worth: someone just pointed out to me that lavaan
was used in a Nature article this week:
http://www.nature.com/srep/2015/150330/srep09521/full/srep09521.html)

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Lavaan - credible software?
messages.subject_clean: Lavaan - credible software?
messages.body_plain:
> "Lavaan only approximates SEM

I'm not sure what this is supposed to mean.  It estimates SEM parameters, just like other SEM software.  They seem to indicate that it is only a "real" SEM if it is fit to data using commercial software, which is just not true.

> and even the creator of the program himself admits that “the results of lavaan are very close … to those reported by their current commercial program” (Rosseel, 2012).

I believe it can mimic results from Mplus, LISREL, and EQS (3 commercial software programs that each can give different results from each other).

> If lavaan does give the same results, then there really is no concern, the problem is, you never know when it may or may not."

Replicability of results is indeed an important facet of scientific progress.  But the fact is that numerous algorithms can be designed to solve the same problem.  Each commercial SEM software package is a different of algorithms for solving (mostly) the same set of problems.  Even if they base their work on the same mathematics, they can translate equations into a program very differently.

lavaan is just as valid as any other package because it is based on the same mathematics behind SEM.  Furthermore, it includes options to mimic the algorithms of Mplus, EQS, and LISREL.  The difference about lavaan is that it is open-source, so you can actually read the program to see what is being done.  It is commerical software that requires faith, whereas lavaan is open to peer-review, making lavaan more conducive to scientific progress than commericial software.

Terry

messages.subject_clean: Lavaan - credible software?
messages.body_plain:
It sounds like your reviewer either (a) has a bias against open source software, (b) has confused a particular package with the analytical method itself, as many people take LISREL to be a method and not just software, or (c) has Lavaan confused with a composite-based method, as this is the kind of complaint one encounters about composite-based methods.
     If it might help . . .the publisher Wiley is putting together an online encyclopedia on research methods called Wiley StatsRef.  I am the author of two revised articles, one titled "Structural Equation Modeling: Software."  The original, published in 2005, of. Or use did not mention lavaan, but the revision places it squarely among other packages for factor-based SEM.  If you like, I can send you a copy of the proof.
--Ed Rigdon

Sent from my iPad

messages.subject: Re: Simulating Ordinal Data
messages.subject_clean: Simulating Ordinal Data
messages.body_plain:
Just a note, I've realized a workaround which makes it much easier. Simply specify a list with both the generative model and the argument paramaterization = "theta", and feed that to simsem instead. Similarly for the specification model:

gen<-list(model=simple.pop.a,parameterization="theta")
mod<-list(model=simple.spec,parameterization="theta")

OutPut<-sim(nRep=1000,model=mod,generate=gen,n=1000,lavaanfun="sem",seed=1234)

I've also found a presentation by Yves which discusses Delta vs Theta parameterization and the implications for scaling factors:

http://www.personality-project.org/r/tutorials/summerschool.14/rosseel_sem_cat.pdf

Now if only multiple groups could be generated in simsem with lavaan syntax! :)

Dear Professor Terrence Jorgensen,

Thank you very much for your advice. Your comments were really helpful. But, I am somewhat confused why existing commercial SEM softwares are using different algorithms in spite of same mathematical solutions. I think I could't understand the difference between algorithms and mathematical equations. Would you please clarify the meaning of algorithms compared to mathematics/equations in your comments below? Then, would you please give me some more advice about why existing SEM softwares are using different algorithms? If it is true, depending on the software researchers use, their results would be differently generated; it would be critical problems I guess.

Thank you very much for your advice in advance.

On Wednesday, April 1, 2015 at 3:07:25 AM UTC-4, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
>
> > "Lavaan only approximates SEM
>
> I'm not sure what this is supposed to mean.  It estimates SEM parameters, just like other SEM software.  They seem to indicate that it is only a "real" SEM if it is fit to data using commercial software, which is just not true.
>
> > and even the creator of the program himself admits that “the results of lavaan are very close … to those reported by their current commercial program” (Rosseel, 2012).
>
> I believe it can mimic results from Mplus, LISREL, and EQS (3 commercial software programs that each can give different results from each other).
>
> > If lavaan does give the same results, then there really is no concern, the problem is, you never know when it may or may not."
>
> Replicability of results is indeed an important facet of scientific progress.  But the fact is that numerous algorithms can be designed to solve the same problem.  Each commercial SEM software package is a different of algorithms for solving (mostly) the same set of problems.  Even if they base their work on the same mathematics, they can translate equations into a program very differently.
>
> lavaan is just as valid as any other package because it is based on the same mathematics behind SEM.  Furthermore, it includes options to mimic the algorithms of Mplus, EQS, and LISREL.  The difference about lavaan is that it is open-source, so you can actually read the program to see what is being done.  It is commerical software that requires faith, whereas lavaan is open to peer-review, making lavaan more conducive to scientific progress than commericial software.
>
> Terry
>

In addition, if you run any complex model in different software you're likely to get (very, very slightly) different answers. That's true of SEM, if you compare (say) LISREL, Mplus and AMOS.   It's even more true when programs have idiosyncratic ways to calculate things - e.g the incrememental fit indices (CFI/NNFI) in Mplus are calculated differently from most other programs.

It's also true of multilevel models. Try running a multilevel logistic model in two packages (or even, in the case of SAS, two procs within the same package) and the results don't always agree perfectly.

J

An example using the Holzinger & Swineford data:

library(lavaan)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
             '

# using full data
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, group="school")
summary(fit)

# Using the sample.cov interface
S.Pasteur <- cov(subset(HolzingerSwineford1939, school=="Pasteur")[,7:15])
S.GrantWhite <- cov(subset(HolzingerSwineford1939,
school=="Grant-White")[,7:15])

fit2 <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov=list(Pasteur=S.Pasteur,
                                       `Grant-White`=S.GrantWhite),
                       sample.nobs=c(156,145), meanstructure=TRUE)
summary(fit2)

Yves.

Hi,

I compared MPLUS, LAVAAN and the R package « SEM » for a structural model with a exogenous formative measurement model.

Eta1: formative latent with four endogenous indicators X1,... X4

Eta2 : reflective endogenous latent with for manifests Y1,... Y4

Eta3 : reflective endogenous latent with for manifests Y5,... Y8

Eta1-> Eta2; Eta1->Eta3

I generated data with a link from X1 to Eta2 (Eta 1 do not mediate the link between X1 and Eta 2) to obtain high MI.

I have some problems with LAVAAN.

 1/ MPLUS, LAVAAN and SEM give same estimations, same chisquare, same standardized solutions,…

 2/ MPLUS and SEM give Rsquare for the formative latent variable, LAVAAN do not:

> inspect(RSLT,"r2")

   Y1    Y2    Y3    Y4    Y5    Y6    Y7    Y8  LAT2  LAT3

0.807 0.814 0.809 0.804 0.809 0.812 0.810 0.812 0.362 0.359

Error in `rownames<-`(`*tmp*`, value = c("LAT2", "LAT3")) :

  length of 'dimnames' [1] not equal to array extent

messages.body_plain:
On 04/03/2015 02:42 PM, Hervé DE BREST wrote:
>   2/ MPLUS and SEM *give Rsquare for the formative latent variable*,
> LAVAAN do not:

That is by design. The '<~' operator is only supposed to be used for
'formative' latent variables in the strict sense, implying: "no residual
error".

If you want to allow for a residual error for your 'LAT1' latent
variable, you need to replace the '<~' formula by this:

     LAT1 =~ 0
     LAT1 ~  1*X1+X2+X3+X4

Yves.

As a general comment: the 'growth()' function of lavaan was only
designed for

1) growth-in-the-observed-variables setting (not growth in the latent
variables), and

2) continuous observed variables.

(I seriously consider removing it from lavaan 0.6, but adding a new
operator instead that defines random effects.)

I would recommend using the lavaan() function for this, perhaps in
combination with some auto.*= arguments. (see ?lavaan)

So, try to code the growth model in such a way that you are very
explicit about every parameter that you need in the model, use the
lavaan() function, and that should do it.

Yves.

messages.subject: Population level fit function... how does it work in lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: Population level fit function... how does it work in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
Hello. I'm trying to teach myself some more advanced concepts when it comes to fit in SEM and the one I am working with right now is the population-level fit function for traditional, multivariate normal theory (so the simplest one). The way I understand this (I might be wrong) is that if you were to put the population covariance matrix and the model-implied covariance matrix in the function, the resulting number (after taking logarithms, determinants and inverses) would be what the population-level minimum of the fit function is.

Unfortunately for me, when I tried doing this for simulated data, the values I obtain are pretty different. Here is the example I'm working with. I'm using the psych package because it has a clean 'tr()' function for the trace of a matrix.

This is the code I use to obtain the population covariance matrix:

library(lavaan)
library(psych)
library(simsem)

mod1 <- 'f1 =~ 0.7*y1 + 0.7*y2 +0.7*y3 +0.7*y4
         f2 =~ 0.7*y5 + 0.7*y6 +0.7*y7 +0.7*y8

         f1 ~~ 0.3*f2

         f1 ~~ 1*f1
         f2 ~~ 1*f2'

dat1  <- simulateData(mod1,1, return.fit=TRUE)
pop.sigm  <- fitted(attr(dat1, 'fit'))$cov

This is the one I am using for the model-implied covariance matrix. As you can see there are two differences from the previous one: variable 'y1' is measuring f2 instead of f1 AND the factors are uncorrelated

mod2 <- 'f1 =~ 0.7*y2 +0.7*y3 +0.7*y4
         f2 =~ 0.7*y5 + 0.7*y6 +0.7*y7 +0.7*y8 + 0.7*y1

         f1 ~~ 0.0*f2

         f1 ~~ 1*f1
         f2 ~~ 1*f2'

dat2  <- simulateData(mod2,1, return.fit=TRUE)
mod.sigm    <- fitted(attr(dat2, 'fit'))$cov

Now, from what I understand if I substitute 'pop.sigm' and 'mod.sigm' into the normal likelihood fit function, that would be the population-level fit function. So something like this:

> log(det(pop.sigm))+tr((pop.sigm%*%solve(mod.sigm)))-log(det(mod.sigm))-dim(mod.sigm)[1]
[1] 0.3772527

Now, I thought that if I ran a simulation where mod1 is the 'population' covariance matrix and mod2 is what is being fitted, the average of the minimized fit functions would be close to 0.3772527. But it is not :(

fit.mod <- 'f1 =~ NA*y2 +y3 +y4
            f2 =~ NA*y5 + y6 +y7 +y8 +y1

            f1 ~~ 0.0*f2

            f1 ~~ 1*f1
            f2 ~~ 1*f2'

simu1 <- sim(1000, fit.mod, n=1000, generate=mod1, lavaanfun="sem")
simuf <- simu1@fit$fmin

> mean(simuf)
[1] 0.1298477

In this case, 0.129847 is not even remotely close to 0.3772527 and it doesn't really matter how much I increase the number of replications or the sample size, there is always a big difference between those two.

Hi Elia,

Instead of

tr((pop.sigm %*% solve(mod.sigm)))

You should have

tr((mod.sigm %*% solve(pop.sigm)))

Also, if you have a mean-structure (which I believe may be the default when using simsem), then you need to add this term to your fit function (see attachment):

... + t(mod.means - pop.means) %*% solve(pop.sigm) %*% (mod.means - pop.means)

You can check whether your results have a mean structure by printing

head(simu1@coef)

Terry

Thank you Terry! That was a really good catch :)

I changed that part on the fit function, generated AND fitted my data expressively specifying 'meanstructure=FALSE' and worked a small simulation outside of simsem. Although the results are better now, they're by no means close :(

Apparently, the sample minimized fit function statistic is not a good estimate of its population analog (or so I read while working on this) so I decided to work directly with the population definition of RMSEA (square root of the minimized fit function divided by degrees of freedom of the model). So here is what I did now. I used the same code as before to generate the population and model-implied covariance matrices (specifying meanstructure=FALSE wherever I could) and proceeded like this:

fit.mod <- 'f1 =~ NA*y2 +y3 +y4
            f2 =~ NA*y5 + y6 +y7 +y8 +y1

            f1 ~~ 0.0*f2

            f1 ~~ 1*f1
            f2 ~~ 1*f2'

### small simulation and a vector to store the sample estimates of RMSEA
rmzea <- double(1000)

for (i in 1:1000) {
datz <- simulateData(mod1, sample.nobs=1000)
rmzea[i] <- as.numeric(fitMeasures(cfa(fit.mod, data=datz, meanstructure=FALSE), "rmsea"))
}

### minimized fit function corrected as per your suggestion
F  <- log(det(pop.sigm))+tr((mod.sigm%*%solve(pop.sigm)))-log(det(mod.sigm))-dim(mod.sigm)[1]
df <- as.numeric(fitMeasures(sem(fit.mod, sample.cov=pop.sigm, sample.nobs=1000), "df"))

> sqrt(F/df)
[1] 0.1545489
> mean(rmzea)
[1] 0.1094027

So it is *a lot* closer, but still a little far off from the average of the samples. Unfortunately I tried it with even more grossly misspecified models and the difference between those two is worse, with the 'population version' always higher than the average across the samples.

Do I need to adjust for mean structure even if I explicitly declared them as 'FALSE'?

The output which I receive is somewhat odd in that the degrees of freedom are incorrect, though, and in order for lavaan to correctly estimate what the nonlinearly constrained loadings are, I needed ot start it out with a very favorable initial estimate.

messages.subject: Re: Population level fit function... how does it work in lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: Population level fit function... how does it work in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
Woops, I should have caught this the first time.  What you are calculating as F is not the "population" minimum fit function because you are comparing the Sigmas of 2 populations, when it should be the discrepancy between the Sigma of 1 population and the ESTIMATE of that Sigma if another model is fit to the true Sigma.  You define one of the populations (pop.sigm) arbitrarily as THE population covariance matrix (Sigma), and your treat the other population covariance matrix (mod.sigm) as though it were your model's best-possible (ML) estimate of Sigma.  But S is not a function of the true population parameters of a different model; instead, S is the covariance matrix implied by estimates of parameters when a particular model (in your case, fit.mod) is fit to data from a different population (in your case, data = pop.sigm).

Long story short, your use of the sim() function is correctly executed to return the information you want.  The average of the minimum fit function (F) when a target model (fit.mod) is fit to data from a different population (pop.mod) should approximate your "population" RMSEA for that target model fit to that population.  But your calculation of the population RMSEA is incorrect.  To calculate the population RMSEA, you merely need to fit the (incorrect) target model to the population covariance matrix (i.e., the data without sampling error) --
fitMeasures(cfa(fit.mod, sample.cov = pop.sigm, sample.nobs = 1000, meanstructure=FALSE), "rmsea")
The level of N is inconsequential because it is removed from the chi-squared (N * F) in the formula for RMSEA, but I put 1000 above because that is what you used in your finite samples using sim().  If you run your simulation again, this value should be MUCH closer to your mean RMSEA across 1000 samples.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
I think the similarity is a coincidence, as you suspect.  All your factor loadings are 0.7 in both populations, so the 2 population covariance matrices don't look all that different.  If you chose very different population values for the second population model, then the discrepancy between the 2 populations would be much larger.  But RMSEA is not the discrepancy between 2 populations. It is the discrepancy between a true population and the best estimate of that population using a model that may or may not have the correct functional form.

One more thing.  If you are comparing the mean RMSEA across samples to the population RMSEA, it will be a biased estimate at smaller sample sizes (at least when misspecification is not huge) because the formula places a lower bound at 0.  This article is pretty informative:

dx.doi.org/10.1177/0049124103256130 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/0049124103256130>

Terry

> How can one code for a multigroup model in which a parameter is fixed in some groups and free in others?  For instance, if we have 2 groups and want the path xày to be fixed in one group but free in the other, who would one specify this?

A missing value (NA) frees a parameter, and a scalar fixes a parameter.  For multiple groups, use a vector (1 element per group) instead of a single value in the syntax.

y ~ c(1, NA)*x

More specifically, when the causal model for some groups is a subset of the causal model in other groups (i.e. some variables aren’t found in some groups)? messages.subject: Re: Reporting Regression Results from SEM output
messages.subject_clean: Reporting Regression Results from SEM output
messages.body_plain:
Hi

You can get R2’s using the summary-method. See http://www.jstatsoft.org/v48/i02/paper

The z-statistic, which you can see in your results, is calculated in the exact same way as the t-statistic and they are also nearly identically distributed if sample size is over 30 or so. In regression, the sampling distribution of the ratio of estimated coefficients and SEs follows the t-distribution in small samples when the model assumptions hold. The problem with more complex models, such as SEMs, is that the proofs exists only for large sample scenarios, which would lead to z-statistic. Therefore, reporting t-statistics would not be appropriate.

For the same reason I do not think that using the F-statistic is appropriate in SEM context.

Mikko

messages.body_plain:
>
> I want to know how much variance the regression equation can explain.

You mean an r-squared for each predictor?  Look in the "std.all" column for the standardized regression slopes.  Those are semipartial correlation coefficients (r), which you can square if you think that tells you something different from the unsquared r.  Try saving the data.frame returned by parameterEstimates() and adding a column that is the square of the "std.all" column.

But that r-squared can only be interpreted as "the proportion of variance in the outcome explained by that single predictor" when the predictors themselves do not share any variance (r = 0), which (realistically) can only be the case when you have control over the predictors (e.g., balanced random assignment to conditions in a factorial design).

Terry

Hi Alex,

The problem appears to be solved.

My original model syntax contained the following...

#Beta proportions
D2 ~ B*L1
D3 ~ B*L2
D4 ~ B*L3

#Latent intercept / slope loadings
I =~ 1*L1
S =~ A*D2 + A*D3 + A*D4

#constraints
A == 1
B == 0

I changed it to...

#Beta proportions
D2 ~ 0*L1
D3 ~ 0*L2
D4 ~ 0*L3

#Latent intercept / slope loadings
I =~ 1*L1
S =~ 1*D2 + 1*D3 + 1*D4

....and runMI() ran normally, without errors

Since I have such little experience with lavaan, I am not sure if I should have not used "==" in this way,  or if it is something that causes an error with RunMI.

Thanks for your help and sorry to bother you all with something so simple.

Thanks,
Clint

Hi,

I am trying to run a mediation model, with one of the mediators being a binary variable (negative). It resulted in a warning message. Could I still use the results and the model without ordering the variables so that the 'negative' variable can remain in the model?

Return_MK ~ f*MK.sat_mean + d*negative + b*MK.exp_mean

#mediator
MK.exp_mean ~ a*MK.sat_mean
negative ~ c*MK.sat_mean

#indirect effect
sat_neg := c*d
sat_exp := a*b

#mediator correlation
negative ~~ MK.exp_mean

messages.subject_clean: Reporting Regression Results from SEM output
messages.body_plain:
Eafaela—

     The difference between t and z is a matter of sample size—as sample size increases, the t distribution converges on a z distribution.  Factor-based SEM is generally a large sample methodology, so that the distinction between t and z should be minimal.  That is why you only see z values.  (in the old LISREL package, they were called t values, but were really z values even there.)

--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject_clean: Comparing models (re-running models) across many datasets
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,
      I am hoping to write a loop function that will re-run a model in Lavaan based on a grouping variable (here I am using CFA).  e.g., If I have the data from 10 studies in a single dataset (with a factor variable to indicate which rows belong to which studies), I would like to re-run the model for each study then return a table with all the fit indicies. This would also be useful to run models by any subset of the data, e.g., sex, age, etc.

To do this, I have combined all the data into one dataset called "data" and created a variable "Study" which indicates which study the results belong to. Then I am splitting the data by this factor (using the split function), running the model on each object in the list, and extracting the fit indicies of interest (simplifying them by sapply).

I imagine the solution lies in the "apply" loop where the "data"  in the cfa(model, data) is currently a list containing the split data. The function needs to change this (data = Splitdata) to the current value of "i" in the list (Splitdata) that is being looped.

The final line of code that extracts the fits seems to be working fine.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
I have called the data "data", and the grouping variable "Study".

# First we specify the model
Model      <- ' Factor1 =~ var.1 + var.2 + var.3 + var.4
                      Factor 2 =~ var.5 + var.6 + var.7 + var.8 '

# then split the data into a list containing each study's data
Splitdata <- split(data, data$Study)

#Now create a new list containing each model
Cfa.Models <- apply(Splitdata, function(Splitdata) cfa(model, data = Splitdata))

#Finally, we can pull out the desired fit indicies

Cfa.Fits <- sapply(Cfa.Models, function(Cfa.Models) fitMeasures(Cfa.Models, c("chisq", "df","fmin", "cfi", "nnfi", "srmr", "rmsea", "rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "rmsea.pvalue") ))

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Thanks for all of your help with this problem!!!!
            -  Conal

messages.subject_clean: Using a linear regression measurement model within a logistic structural model
messages.body_plain:
> However, when they are later used in a logistic SEM, the latents are being treated as dichotomous (?).

No, lavaan only handles continuous latent variables.  In you model, your predictors are continuous latent variables.  It is the outcome (ExcellentOutcome) that is (I assume) a binary observed variable.

> Is there a way to use both regression techniques within one model? Alternatively, should I refit my measurement model using logit?
>
> #Measurement Model
> Latent1 =~ Item1+Item1+Item3+Item4+Covariate
> Latent2 =~ Item5+Item6+Item7+Item8+Covariate
> #Outcome Model
> ExcellentOutcome~Covariate+Latent1+Latent2
> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
> ExcellentOutcome is a dichotomous variable.
> Item1-8 have 1-4 range

The items have only 4 categories, so you should treat them as ordered when you call lavaan (see the tutorials on the lavaan web site).  By default, lavaan will use a probit link, and if you want to use a logit link, you need to use the MML estimator (see the ?lavaan help page).  Regardless of which link you use, the latent variables are continuous, not categorical.  It is only the outcomes (including indicators) that are categorical.

Terry

messages.subject_clean: group.equal="thresholds" (categorical data measurement invariance) appears to not be acting properly
messages.body_plain:
It helps to have a reproducible example, so I used some data from an Mplus example available online:

myData <- read.table("http://www.statmodel.com/usersguide/chap5/ex5.16.dat")
names(myData) <- c("u1","u2","u3","u4","u5","u6","x1","x2","x3","g")
myData$u1 <- ordered(myData$u1)
myData$u2 <- ordered(myData$u2)
myData$u3 <- ordered(myData$u3)
myData$u4 <- ordered(myData$u4)
myData$u5 <- ordered(myData$u5)
myData$u6 <- ordered(myData$u6)

model <- '
f1 =~ u1 + u2 + u3
f2 =~ u4 + u5 + u6
'

fit0 <- cfa(model, data = myData, ordered = paste0("u", 1:6),
            group = "g", group.equal = c("loadings","thresholds"))
fit1 <- cfa(model, data = myData, ordered = paste0("u", 1:6),
            group = "g", group.equal = "loadings")

The parameter table shows why the degrees of freedom decrease.

partable(fit0)
partable(fit1)

When you constrain only the loadings, the scale parameters (partable(fit0)$op == "~*~") are fixed to 1 in both groups.  When you also constrain the thresholds to equality, the scale parameters are only fixed to 1 in the first group, and estimated for group 2 (in this example).

I am not familiar enough with parameterization and constraints for categorical CFA to know whether this is what is supposed to happen, but I would guess that is what happened with your data, too.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
I have three things here:

1. Df from Terry's example is going down.
2. You should use theta parameterization to run multiple-group categorical CFA. You will deal with item residual variance rather than item scaling parameter.
3. You should write the script for each step manually. Otherwise, you might not test the model you wanted. For example, you need the factor mean in Group 2 to be free in the strong model but this script did not do it automatically.

You could see my website for examples.

http://www.myweb.ttu.edu/spornpra/catInvariance.html

messages.subject_clean: How can I get the output with z- and p- vlaue of variances from latent growth curve analyses?
messages.body_plain:
> While I can find intercept estimates of latent variables with z- and p- values from summary output, however, z- and p- values don't accompany variance estimates of the two latent variables when printing summary output

You can get them from the output of parameterEstimates()

> In addition, anybody who knows how to get p-value of the correlation coefficient between the intercept
> and the slope? I could find correlation coefficient using "inspect" function, but it showed only the coefficient
> without p-value.

You refer to the p value of the covariance (seen in the summary output) to test the null hypothesis that the covariance (and by implication, the correlation) is zero.  You just look at the "std.all" column to interpret the covariance in a more familiar standardized/correlation metric.

It may not be worth the extra effort, but if you really want the correlation to be an actual model parameter, you can use phantom variables for the growth factors:
regress each growth factor on a phantom variable (regression slopes will be the standard deviations of the growth factors)
fix the original growth factor variances (and their covariance) to zero
fix the phantom variable variances to one
the estimated covariance between the phantom variables will be in correlation metric because the phantom variances = 1.
Terry

Yes, it is as follows:

mydata<- read.csv("heis.csv")

myvars <- c("diagnosis","Gender","Speedprocess","Attentionvigil","Workingmem","Verballearn","Visuallearn","Reasonproblem","Socialcog","P1","P2","P3","P4","P5","P6","P7","N1","N2","N3","N4","N5","N6","N7","G1","G2","G3","G4","G5","G6","G7","G8","G9","G10","G11","G12","G13","G14","G15","G16")

newdata

#subset 1
newdata1<-subset(newdata,diagnosis== "1" )
#subset 2
newdata2<-subset(newdata,diagnosis== "2" )
#rbind together
newdata3<-rbind(newdata1,newdata2)

newdata4<-subset(newdata,diagnosis>=1&diagnosis<3)
newdata5<-subset(newdata,Gender=="Female")

rownames(newdata5) <- NULL

newdata5

newdata.model<-'
cognition=~Speedprocess+Attentionvigil+Workingmem+Verballearn+Visuallearn+Reasonproblem+Socialcog
Panssp=~P1+P2+P3+P4+P5+P6+P7
Panssn=~N1+N2+N3+N4+N5+N6+N7
Panssg=~G1+G2+G3+G4+G5+G6+G7+G8+G9+G10+G11+G12+G13+G14+G15+G16
Cognition~Panssp
Cognition~Panssn
Cognition~Panssg
Panssp~Panssn
Panssp~Panssg
Panssn~Panssg'

sem.fit<-sem(newdata.model,data=newdata5)
summary(sem.fit,standardized=TRUE,fit.measures=TRUE)

messages.subject: Re: How can I get the output with z- and p- vlaue of variances from latent growth curve analyses?
messages.subject_clean: How can I get the output with z- and p- vlaue of variances from latent growth curve analyses?
messages.body_plain:
regress each growth factor on a phantom variable (regression slopes will be the standard deviations of the growth factors)
fix the original growth factor variances (and their covariance) to zero
fix the phantom variable variances to one
the estimated covariance between the phantom variables will be in correlation metric because the phantom variances = 1.

model.kor <- '#i and s
i =~ 1*Y1.kor + 1*Y2.kor + 1*Y3.kor
s =~ 0*Y1.kor + 1*Y2.kor + 2*Y3.kor

#1
ph_i =~ i
ph_s =~ s

#2
i ~~ 0*i + 0*s
s ~~ 0*s

#3
ph_i ~~ 1*ph_i
ph_s ~~ 1*ph_s

#4
ph_i ~~ NA*ph_s
'

The fit of the model will be identical, all you do is change the parametarization (you estimate the growth 2 parameters' SDs rather than variances; everything else you add is just fixed parameters).  This text on longitudinal SEM has more examples and discussion of phantom variables:

http://www.guilford.com/books/Longitudinal-Structural-Equation-Modeling/Todd-Little/9781462510160/reviews

Terry

It's hard to tell exactly what you are trying to model.  Are Y1/Y2/Y3 indicators of a latent construct, measured at 3 occasions (pre, mid, and post)?  If so, you should be measuring common factors of items within the same occasion, not common variance of a single item across occasions.

teach.pre =~ a*Y1.pre + b*Y2.pre + c*Y3.pre
teach.mid =~ a*Y1.mid + b*Y2.mid + c*Y3.mid
teach.post <http://teach.post> =~ a*Y1.post + b*Y2.post + c*Y3.post
teach_i =~ 1*teach.pre + 1*teach.mid + 1*teach.post <http://teach.post>
teach_s =~ 0*teach.pre + 1*teach.mid + 2*teach.post <http://teach.post>

Instead, what you currently have are constructs for common variance within an item, but across occasions:

> # effect of teach on attitude

> # Y1/Y2/Y3.teach

> Y1.teach =~ Y1.pre + a*Y1.mid + b*Y1.post

> Y2.teach =~ Y2.pre + a*Y2.mid + b*Y2.post

> Y3.teach =~ Y3.pre + a*Y3.mid + b*Y3.post

> # intercepts & slopes of teach

> teach_i =~ 1*Y1.teach + 1*Y2.teach + 1*Y3.teach

> teach_s =~ 0*Y1.teach + 1*Y2.teach + 2*Y3.teach
>

> What mistake did I make? How could I fix the problem?

I'm not sure exactly what caused the specific error you saw, but if it persists after you change your syntax above, you should post your full R syntax (not just lavaan model syntax) and some data, so that the problem can be reproduced.

You can read more about growth curve models for latent variables in this short text:

http://www.sagepub.com/textbooks/Book229205

> In addition, I'd like know how to constrain covariances among errors/residuals of each time point observation.

You constrain them with labels, the same way you did to constrain intercepts in your model syntax.  (co)variance parameters are specified with the "~~" operator, as you can see in my response to your other post this evening, and in the help page for lavaan syntax:

?lavaanify # type this into your R console

as well as on the lavaan tutorial web pages:

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax2.html

Terry

messages.subject: with multiple groups modindices() in lavaan 0.5-18 behaves differently than in version 0.5-17
messages.subject_clean: with multiple groups modindices() in lavaan 0.5-18 behaves differently than in version 0.5-17
messages.body_plain:
In a model in which two groups are specified and some parameters are constrained to be equal across groups, modification indices behave differently in the new (0.5-18) and in the previous (0.5-17) versions of lavaan.
Version 0.5-17: the indices take the exact same value for the same parameters in group 1 and in group 2. Although I am not an expert, this makes a lot of sense to me.
Version 0.5-18: the values of the modification indices are different among groups.
I don't know whether this is an improvement (if so, I would ask for your advice about how interpret the MIs in similar cases) or a bug (if so, can I trust the MIs in version 0.5-17).

Below you can find a toy example that shows the issue. Please try it with the latest version of lavaan and with the older version.
Thank you very much for your attention,

Giulio Costantini

######################################################################################################
# install version 0.5-17
install.packages("http://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/lavaan/lavaan_0.5-17.tar.gz", repo = NULL, type = "source")
# install latest version
#install.packages("lavaan")
library(lavaan)
library(MASS)

# simulate the data for two groups
set.seed(1)
cormat1 <- cormat2 <-  matrix(.4, nrow = 4, ncol = 4)
diag(cormat1) <- diag(cormat2) <- 1
cormat2[1,2] <- cormat2[2,1] <- .1 # introduce a clear difference among the groups

data1 <- mvrnorm(n = 100,
                 mu = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
                 Sigma = cormat1)
data2 <- mvrnorm(n = 100,
                 mu = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
                 Sigma = cormat2)
data <- data.frame(rbind(data1, data2))
data$group <- c(rep(1, 100), rep(2, 100))

# define a toy moel, in which the covariances are
# constrained to be equal
model <- '
X1 ~~ c(a1, a1)*X2 + c(a2, a2)*X3 + c(a3, a3)*X4
X2 ~~ c(a4, a4)*X3 + c(a5, a5)*X4
X3 ~~ c(a6, a6)*X4
X1 ~~ a7*X1
X2 ~~ a8*X2
X3 ~~ a9*X3
X4 ~~ a9*X4'

# fit the model with lavaan
fit1 <- sem(model = model, data = data, group = "group",
    meanstructure = FALSE)

modindices(fit1)
########################################################################################################

messages.subject: Not being positive definite
messages.subject_clean: Not being positive definite
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,

This is my first attempt of CFA, so any help is very much appreciated.

I have 9 observed variables; they can be grouped into three groups (3 in each) measuring 3 latent variables. I am trying to follow the logic of Miyake (2000) paper to show that there is commonality but also diversity of the three latent variables.  So the first step is to test following models: (1) three latent variables were orthogonal, fixed to 0 (diversity model); (2) three latent variable were perfectly correlated, fixed to 1 (unity model); (3) correlation between latent variables were free to estimate.

First, the model where latent covariance can be estimated freely converged without warnings.

modelC <-‘

updating =~ Task1 + Task4 + Task6

inhibition =~ Task3 + Task7 + Task9

shifting =~ Task2 + Task5 + Task8’

fit.modelC<- cfa(modelC, data = EF.data.M,)

However, when I tried to fit the model with orthogonal latent variables:

fit.modelC.orth<- cfa(modelC, data = EF.data.M, orthogonal = TRUE)

it generated warning messages “covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite” and “some estimated variances are negative”

I wonder what the problem is and how am I able to get around this? I have checked discussions about matrix not being positive definite. It has mentioned that this could be due to model misspecification or missing values which were not the case. Also it mentioned linear dependency could be a problem, this is neither the case, in addition, the fact that modelC without assuming orthogonality converged successfully means the covariance matrix is positive definite (am I correct with this?).

Many thanks in advance for any input/comment.

messages.subject: RE: Not being positive definite
messages.subject_clean: Not being positive definite
messages.body_plain:
First, if the freely estimated factor covariances were substantial, then the orthogonality model will be a very poor fit to the data, and very strange things can happen when the model is a very poor fit.  Second, with orthogonality constraints in place, statistical identification (the ability to obtain unique best estimates of parameters) in your model—with three indicators for each common factor—hinges on *every* factor loading being “large.”  If even one loading is not “large,” then identification fails, and you cannot trust output in any way.  There is no guarantee that you can obtain what you may call “good” estimates from the orthogonality model.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: Re: cfa: correlation matrix with communalities diagonally
messages.subject_clean: cfa: correlation matrix with communalities diagonally
messages.body_plain:
Sounds like you are operating in an EFA framework, not CFA.  I've never heard of anyone considering this relevant outside of EFA, so I'm not sure why you'd need them for a model fitted with lavaan, but it would be trivial to calculate yourself.  Communalities are the sum of squared (standardized) factor loadings, so if you have no cross-loadings in your model, then you can just square the factor loadings in the "std.all" column of the parameterEstimates() output, then use the diag() function to replace the diagonal of your observed correlation matrix with those values.  But it is not available from lavaan output (e.g., using the inspect() function), nor do I see why it would be expected.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Beinan--
     "Large" is something like "statistically significant," though significance is arbitrary, based on choice of alpha.  Basic identification rules are:

3 indicators per factor, or
2 indicators per factor, if each factor is correlated with something else (like another factor).

     My guess is that the weak Loadings mean that you cannot estimate the orthogonality model conventionally.  Given that, I do not have a way for you to achieve the kind of parallel that you want.
     As you guess, taking away an indicator with a weak loading does not help the problem.
     3 per factor is not "ideal" by any means.  It is just the minimum that achieves identification, without some other constraints being added.  More indicators is better for firmly establishing the factors.  (When you have time, search for the phrase, "factor indeterminacy.")
--Ed Rigdon

Sent from my iPad
